newsitem.title: USA: U.S. told Bosnia official to be replaced.
newsitem.headline: U.S. told Bosnia official to be replaced.

text.p: Bosnia told the United States on Friday it would meet U.S. demands next week for firing Bosnian Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic as a condition of delivering $100 million in military hardware to Sarajevo, U.S. and Bosnia officials said.
The pledge came during a meeting between Bosnia's U.N. ambassador, Mohammed Sacirbey, and Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum, the U.S. special envoy on Bosnia.
"A course of action has been set up where we feel pretty comfortable these issues can be resolved in the next couple of days," Sacirbey told reporters at the State Department.
"There's a clear commitment to make it work," he said, adding that action by the United States -- which he did not specify -- is also needed.

A U.S. official confirmed that Sacirbey indicated the issue would be resolved early next week with the swearing-in by parliament of a replacement for Cengic and another defence official whose removal Washington also sought.

The two men are viewed as too close to Iran -- which the United States considers a state sponsor of terrorism -- as well as obstacles to building central government institutions viewed as critical to a new unified postwar Bosnia.

"When in fact the problem has been solved and when new people are sworn in, then we would consider it appropriate to move forward" with delivering the military hardware, said the U.S. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

He was puzzled that Sacirbey said some action by Washington was also needed. "I didn't commit us to any pre-action," he said, adding that Washington had learned in Bosnia not to take any steps based only on assurances, rather than concrete action, by rival Moslem, Serb and Croat factions.
The Kornblum-Sacirbey meeting took place hours after State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns publicly identified Cengic as the target of American concern.

U.S. officials said privately last week the equipment would not be handed over until Cengic was fired because of his alleged ties with Iran. But Burns said Washington was now going public because Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation failed to meet promises to sack him. Under the Dayton peace accord, Bosnia was divided into the Federation and a Serb entity.
"The United States has determined that Bosnian Federation Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic personally maintains close ties to Iran," Burns told a news briefing.
"He has also obstructed development of the Western-oriented defence structure in the Federation, and he's worked against a democratic Federation in general."

"While senior Bosnian officials have assured us that Mr Cengic will be replaced, the United States has decided that the $100 million worth of equipment ... will not be delivered to the Federation until Mr Cengic is relieved of his responsibilities formally and publicly," Burns said.

The bulk of the equipment, which includes tanks, artillery and helicopters, arrived last week by ship at the Croatian port of Ploce, but the vessel has since moved offshore pending resolution of the Cengic dispute.
The hardware is being supplied under an "equip-and-train" programme whereby Washington hopes to bring the Federation up to the level of the militarily-superior Bosnian Serbs.
The U.S. decision to go fully public with the demand for Cengic's head ratcheted up the pressure on Sarajevo following the failure so far of diplomatic efforts to oust him.

"I've been withholding his name for a week now because we have a commitment from the Bosnian government that he will be relieved of his duties, but we've not seen any action toward this," Burns said. Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic was told of U.S. concerns more than a week ago, he added.

Far from complying, Bosnia's Defence Ministry said on Tuesday the U.S. demand had come "as a complete surprise" after U.S. President Bill Clinton certified in August that Bosnia had met all conditions for the equip-and-train programme to begin.
It said the new conditions "could give rise to suspicions developing between friendly nations which in the final analysis would not be beneficial for either of them."
